title: Execution Models: Trading the Deflection
categoryDescription: Tier 2 - Gamma awareness, pattern recognition, and execution

sections.title: Execution Is the Edge
sections.introContent:
You’ve learned:

- How to read structure
- How to identify regimes
- How to recognize patterns

Now we focus on the only thing that produces PnL:

> **Execution**
> 

We can identify direction and potential pivot points based off the maps. But it wont matter if we cant *execute.*

---

Most traders fail here.

***Not because they don’t see the setup, but because they freeze up when it comes time to deliver.***

---

sections.title: The Execution Doctrine
sections.introContent:
This chapter is built on one rule:

> **We see the setup on the map → price approaches the node → we enter at the direct tap → deflection plays out in our favor**

We are not reacting to a move that already happened. We are reading the map, identifying where dealer pressure is concentrated, and positioning ourselves _at_ the pressure point before the deflection occurs. The pattern is the prediction. The direct tap is the entry.

![Note: Node tests can deflect within a +/- 50 cent range on QQQ and SPY and a 5 dollar range on SPX.](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image.png)

Note: Node tests can deflect within a +/- 50 cent range on QQQ and SPY and a 5 dollar range on SPX.

When looking to execute:

-   Node deflections are not perfect.
    
    -   We do not always reject to the cent.
        
    -   Deflection zones are +/- 50 cents on QQQ and SPY and +/- 5 dollars on SPX in either direction.
        

> Example:
> 
> -   If QQQ has a king node at 590, our deflection zone and entry trigger ranges from 589.50 to 590.50
>     
> -   If SPX has a king node at 6900, our deflection zone and entry trigger ranges from 6895 to 6905.
>     

## Entries must be in line with asymmetric risk to reward.

-   Asymmetric risk to reward: your stop loss is tight and your take profit is generous.
    

> Stop losses off node deflections typically get triggered if we break and hold 1 node above/below the node we are playing a deflection off of.
> 
> -   Example: If we are playing puts off a deflection of 660 SPY gatekeeper node, we would be stopped out on a break and hold above 661.
>     

* * *

### What This Means

We are NOT:

-   Buying support blindly
    
-   Shorting resistance blindly
    
-   Executing outside of context
    
-   Taking trades without cross-index alignment
    
-   Waiting for the move to happen and then chasing it
    

We are:

> Predicting the deflection based on structural evidence and entering at the direct tap

The maps give us the thesis. Patterns like rugs and reverse rugs tell us _where_ dealer pressure will force a reaction. We step in at that moment — buying puts into rug setups as retail chases upside, buying calls into reverse rugs as retail panic sells — and we get filled on their liquidity.

**_We enter at the direct tap of major nodes and wait for reshuffle to occur in our favor._**

![image.png](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image-1.png)

* * *

### The Edge - Key Takeaway

> **We act at the direct tap of major nodes.**

Not before. Not after. This is what gives us near-zero drawdown entries — we are buying into the panic, absorbing liquidity that is being forced out at the extreme, and getting filled as cheap as possible.

sections.title: What Actually Creates the Deflection
sections.introContent:
This is where most education fails.

Deflections are not random.

They are driven by:

- Dealer hedge rebalancing
- Liquidity imbalances
- Forced dealer repositioning

---

### What Happens at Extremes

At key nodes:

- Retail traders get liquidated
- Positions unwind and reshuffle
- Dealers adjust exposure to balance their order books

---

> **This creates the reversal — not the level itself**
> 

---

### The Opportunity

> Retail exits emotionally at the extreme. We are already there, absorbing that liquidity.
> 

This is not a reaction play. We see the setup forming on the map — a rug, a reverse rug, a key node with magnitude — and we know where dealers are likely to defend. When price arrives at that level, retail is panicking out and we are stepping in. Thats how you get cheap fills with minimal drawdown.

---

### "Cheap Fill" — Defined Properly

A cheap fill is:

> **Being positioned at the node as panic liquidity floods the market, not paying into momentum after the move is already underway**
> 

When you buy puts at a rug setup ceiling as price taps it, you are buying from people who are still chasing calls. When you buy calls at a reverse rug floor as price taps it, you are buying from people dumping in fear. Thats the edge — you get filled on their emotion.

---

sections.title: Visual Walkthrough — Node Interaction
sections.introContent:
* * *

### Step 1 — Approach

Price moves toward a high-magnitude node where you have already identified a setup on the map.

You are ready. You have your thesis, your pattern, your cross-index alignment. You are waiting for price to arrive at the level you identified.

* * *

### Step 2 — Deflection

Price taps the node.

[We enter puts off a deflection of SPYs king node + SPX barney ceilings, both of whichpreventing QQQ upside.](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-step_2_-_interaction.mov)

Upon approach, we enter upon a direct tap of a major node or ceiling.

* * *

### Step 2a — Overshoot (IF NEGATIVE GAMMA NODE)

Price pushes beyond.

Retail becomes aggressive.

* * *

### _Overshoot + Stall_

Momentum begins to slow. Map reshuffle begins. Price moves away from the extreme.

Price begins to move away from the extreme.

sections.title: Node Tap Probability (CRITICAL)
sections.introContent:
This is one of the most important execution filters.

The Rule

- **1st Tap of a major node → ~80% reaction probability**
- **2nd Tap of a major node → ~66% reaction probability**
- **3rd Tap of a major node → ~33% reaction probability**

---

### What This Means

Each interaction weakens the level.

Liquidity gets consumed.

---

![image.png](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image-3.png)

---

### Execution Implication

- First test = highest quality fade
- Second test = still tradable
- Third test = **low-quality setup**

---

> **If you are trading the third tap, you are trading a weakening level**
> 

---

sections.title: Midpoint Rule — Where Traders Lose Money
sections.introContent:
This is non-negotiable:

> **Do NOT trade the midpoint between nodes**

![image.png](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image-4.png)

* * *

### Why?

Midpoints are:

-   Dealer rebalancing zones
    
-   Low clarity
    
-   High chop
    

* * *

### _Midpoint Chop_

![image.png](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image-5.png)

* * *

### Rule

> If you are not at an extreme, you do not have an edge (literally).

* * *

sections.title: Regime-Based Execution
sections.introContent:
---

## 🟡 Positive Gamma (Compression)

Behavior:

- Slower movement
- Cleaner reactions
- Mean reversion dominant

---

### Execution

- Fade extremes
- Expect controlled reactions
- Quick in and out

---

> Precision matters here.
> 

---

## 🟣 Negative Gamma (Expansion)

Behavior:

- Fast movement
- Overshoots
- Aggressive extensions

---

### Core Rule

> **It is safer to assume overshoot first.**
> 

---

### Why?

Because this is where traders get run over.

---

### Execution

1. Recognize the overshoot risk before it happens — this is negative gamma, price will likely push through
2. If price overshoots, the thesis is not invalidated — its actually strengthening. Retail is piling in on the wrong side
3. Enter at the extreme as the overshoot stalls. You are buying into trapped participants

---

> You are positioning at the point of maximum panic, not chasing the move after it reverses
> 

---

sections.title: Risk Management — A+ Standard
sections.introContent:
---

### Requirements

1. Chart structure
2. Heatseeker confluence
3. Asymmetric R:R

---

### Risk/Reward

- **3:1 = standard, aim for higher**
- **2:1 = acceptable but not ideal**
- Below = avoid

---

sections.title: How to define stop losses when playing deflections:
sections.introContent:
---

### Core Rule

> **One node beyond invalidation**
> 

---

### *Stops*

![image.png](https://d95fp8dfaxyli.cloudfront.net/academy/ch6-image-6.png)

---

Example:

- Node = 603
- Entry = deflection off 603

Stop:

> Above 604 (break + hold)
> 

---

### Add Chart Confluence

- *Swing levels - prior highs and lows of trends tend to have resting liquidity.*
- *Support / Resistance oftentime lines up with key nodes.*
- Double bottoms / tops

---

sections.title: Execution Rules (Non-Negotiable)
sections.introContent:
-   DO NOT ❌:
    
-   Do NOT trade midpoints ❌
    
-   Do NOT chase moves ❌
    
-   Do NOT trade the third tap aggressively ❌
    

-   DO ✅:
    
-   Assume or be cautious of potential overshoot in negative gamma deflections ✅
    
-   Enter at the direct tap — the pattern is the prediction, the node is the trigger ✅
    

* * *

> No setup, no entry. We dont force trades — we let the map bring price to us.
> 
> -   If the setup doesnt materialize or price never reaches the node, there is no trade
>     

* * *

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.introContent:
- We **predict deflections** based on structural evidence from the maps
- Edge comes from **precision + conviction** — entering at the tap, not chasing after
- Extremes provide opportunity because thats where we absorb panic liquidity
- Midpoints destroy edge
- The best fills come from buying into fear and selling into greed, directly at the node

---

sections.title: Final Principle
sections.introContent:
---

> **You are paid for being precise — and precision means being there when the node gets tapped, not showing up after the move already started.**
> 

---
